newsitem.title: CHINA: Most dead, injured prised from China train wreck.
newsitem.headline: Most dead, injured prised from China train wreck.

text.p: Rescue workers on Wednesday dug through the tangled wreckage of two trains that crashed in central China, killing at least 67 people and injuring more than 260.

Rescuers toiled all Tuesday and through the night to search the twisted carriages lying across the track at Rongjiawan station in central Hunan, a government official in the nearby county town of Yueyang said by telephone.
By early morning on Wednesday they had prised most of the dead and injured from the wreckage.
"The rescue workers are still digging for people," said one witness reached by telephone at Rongjiawan station, some 1,350 km (840 miles) south of Beijing.

The crowded No 324 passenger train, travelling north on the main trunk line between Beijing and the southern boomtown of Guangzhou, crashed into the back of the stationary No 818 late on Tuesday morning, the Yueyang official said.

Local officials placed the death toll in China's bloodiest train accident for several years at 67 by 1.00 a.m. on Wednesday (1700 GMT Tuesday), with more than 260 injured. At least 90 of the injured were in serious condition, officials said.
The casualty toll could have been much higher, but heavy rain at the time of the crash prevented a fire, officials said.
"God blessed us," he said. "There was an explosion when the trains crashed but the heavy rain prevented the big fire that would certainly have happened otherwise."
"The explosion sounded like a huge bomb," the witness said.

Most of the casualties were on board the No 324 train travelling from the southwestern city of Kunming, capital of Yunnan province, to Zhengzhou, capital of central Henan province. All three drivers of the train were killed, the official said.
The stationary train was on its way from the Hunan town of Linxiang to the provincial capital, Changsha.
Some of the casualties were travellers waiting on the Rongjiawan platform, the official said.
The force of the collision sent carriages rearing up onto the station platform, crushing to death or injuring waiting passengers, he said. The collision derailed 13 carriages.
Officials had failed to find the chief guard aboard the Kunming train, the Yueyang official said. "He seems to have disappeared," he said.
The station had been sealed off and was expected to remain closed for several days. Local authorities had also declared a blackout on news reports of the disaster, officials said.

More than 1,100 police and medical workers had rushed to the scene to help with rescue work, officials said. Hospitals at Rongjiawan were packed with injured and some had been sent to the city of Yueyang, 50 km (30 miles) to the north, for treatment.
"There are alot of broken bones and some head injuries," said an official at a hospital in Rongjiawan that had admitted 120 of the injured. An estimated 50 to 60 were seriously hurt.

Officials were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary reports showed failure to switch the points for the Kunming to Zhengzhou train might have been to blame. It was not yet known if human error was involved, they said.
Traffic on the main Beijing-Guangzhou line was unaffected because trains had been switched to the three other tracks.

The crash comes less than a month after China upgraded the speed of its trains, which have for years travelled at a snail's pace. China's trains accelerated on April 1, with those on the main Beijing-Guangzhou line speeding up to 140 kph (84 mph) -- the fastest in China -- from a previous 97 kph (58 mph).
Rail remains the most popular method of transport in China and China's trains are usually extremely crowded, with long-distance trains carrying as many as 1,000 passengers.
Safety on China's railways has improved in recent years after a series of bad crashes in the mid-1980s when hundreds of people were killed.
